name: Priya Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to tech companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To begin, what's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the growing and livestock lead at Hollin Community Farm. It's 30 hectares owned by a community land trust, which means local people own it together. We do vegetables for a weekly box scheme with about 180 households, plus 200 laying hens, a dozen pigs and some sheep that graze the orchard. Mornings are hens and pigs, then I'm in the polytunnels or on the tractor, and I finish by planning next week's harvest list.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in all that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, honestly. I've got soil sensors in the tunnels sending alerts to my phone, and I use an AI assistant to plan crop rotations and write the box newsletter. It saves me about five hours a week. My partner Lena teases me that I talk to the chatbot more than to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of a let-down, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, because I like the tools. But I'd also say it's fine, the farm's problems were never about technology. It's about land prices and getting people to pay what food really costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the farm's finances worry me more than AI ever did. Our box scheme lost about 20 households last year when the cost of living went up. We're leaning on a lottery grant that ends in 2028. My job only exists while the trust can pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools I've got and try a new one or two, like a hen house camera that spots sick birds. I'd help the trust apply for the next grant now, not in 2028. And I'd keep our savings at about three months, maybe build a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little flat. And quietly worried about the grant running out, but that's my normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the grant wasn't renewed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trust would probably cut my hours to four days, and I'd look for part-time work at the big dairy near Kirkby. We'd manage on Lena's wage for a while, but not happily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Lena's work change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Lena handles insurance claims at an office in Kirkby, and some of the routine checking would get automated. Lena says it's mostly copying numbers from one screen to another anyway.

say: I'd admit I'm a little **disappointed**, because I like the tools.
I'd say the farm's problems are **land prices** and the real cost of food.
think: Our **lottery grant** ends in 2028, and my wage depends on it.
The box scheme **lost 20 households** last year as living costs rose.
do: Try a **hen house camera** that spots sick birds early.
Help the trust write the **next grant** application now.
Keep savings at **three months** and add a little more.
feel: A little **flat**, with a quiet, familiar worry about the **grant**.
S0.quote: Our box scheme lost about 20 households last year when the cost of living went up.
fieldNote: Her real risk is the **grant cliff** in 2028, not AI.
She is a keen **AI user** who is let down rather than relieved.
Lena's **office job** would be lightly touched even here.

steps.text: Install a camera in the hen house that spots sick birds
Help the trust write the next lottery grant application now
Add a little each month to the three months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's the one I half expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this could be brilliant for small farms if we share the kit, and terrible if only the giant estates get it. I'd say the land trusts should club together and buy weeding robots as a group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my own job, it's mostly good news. The planning and the newsletter get easier, and robots for weeding come slowly. The thing I really worry about is Lena. Writing, checking and answering customers is basically Lena's whole job, and her team's already been told not to expect new hires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the trust to trial a solar weeding robot next spring, shared with two other farms. We'd save harder, going from three to five months, in case Lena's hours get cut. And I'd join the landworkers' union, because if we're changing how farms work, workers should be in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited about the farm, scared for Lena. Both at once, which is strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena if her team got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena she's the cleverest person I know and that a claims office is a small box for that. Then I'd probably say we can live on my wage plus savings for six months while she figures it out. I'd mean it, but it would be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money gets tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. We'd sell Lena's car and share mine, and the gym memberships go. We don't spend much anyway, we're not fancy people.

say: I'd say shared kit makes this **brilliant** for small farms.
I'd urge land trusts to **club together** and buy weeding robots.
think: My own work gains: **planning and newsletters** get easier with AI.
Lena's **claims job** is exactly the work on that card.
do: Trial a **solar weeding robot** next spring, shared with two farms.
Grow savings from three to **five months** in case Lena's hours drop.
Join the **landworkers' union** to have a say in farm changes.
feel: **Excited** about the farm and **scared** for Lena at once.
S1.quote: Writing, checking and answering customers is basically Lena's whole job, and her team's already been told not to expect new hires.
fieldNote: The household risk sits with her partner's **desk job**, not her own.
She is an **early adopter** who wants farm robots shared, not owned by estates.
She plans concrete **cuts**: one car and the gym.

steps.text: Trial a solar weeding robot next spring with two other farms
Sell Lena's car and build savings to five months
Join the landworkers' union this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. Okay. That's a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to move now: a basic income, or at least proper support for people losing work. And land and robots should be owned by communities, not a handful of companies. I'd post that everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, Lena's job goes in 2028, I'm fairly sure. Then I'd have three years before robots can do what I do in the tunnels and the pig pens. So for a while I'd be the one earner on a farm worker's wage, with rent in Kirkby, and then maybe not even that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in farm robotics at the agricultural college next autumn, so I'm the one who runs the machines. We'd stop the house deposit plan and keep every penny as cash. If it got bad, we'd move in with Lena's parents, who have a big house in Thornby. And I'd campaign hard for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the excited one, but AGI in two years is too fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me more than Lena. The planning side of my job, the rotations and orders, goes in 2028, which honestly I'd hand over gladly. The hands-on part buys me until about 2031, enough to retrain if I start the day the news breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You love AI tools. Does this change how you feel about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I still think the tools are amazing. I just never pictured them turning up in my own house and taking Lena's job.

say: I'd call for **basic income** or proper support for people losing work.
I'd argue land and robots should be **community owned**.
think: I expect Lena's job to **go in 2028**, leaving me as sole earner.
Robots could reach my **tunnels and pens** around 2031.

Pause the **house deposit** plan and keep every penny in cash.
Move in with **Lena's parents** in Thornby if money runs short.
feel: **Alarmed**, even as the usually excited one, because it's **too fast**.
S2.quote: I'm usually the excited one, but AGI in two years is too fast even for me.
fieldNote: Her own adaptability **can't offset** a partner's sudden job loss.
The **three-year gap** is the window she uses to retrain into robotics.
She still loves the tools, which makes the **betrayal** feel personal.

steps.text: Start a part-time farm robotics course at the college next autumn
Pause the house deposit and hold all savings as cash
Move in with Lena's parents in Thornby if money runs out
Campaign for a basic income with the landworkers' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. More room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years, so let's spend them building co-ops that own the robots and retraining people properly. I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means Lena can see it coming and move first. She's been talking about training as a teacher, and that's more about people than paperwork. For me, robots around 2034 means I'd be 35, with time to become the farm's robot person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the farm robotics course over two years at the college, part-time. I'd get the trust to buy one robot weeder by 2029 and let me run it, so I learn on the job. And I'd help set up a regional co-op of land trusts to share machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a useful way. Like the night before lambing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trust can't afford a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the co-op has to. That's the whole point of joining up. One robot weeder shared across four farms is about a quarter of a wage each, which our trust could manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lena about teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena to start the teacher training in 2027, not 2030. Five years sounds long, but courses fill up once everyone's scared.

I'd be **organising** meetings, not just posting online.
think: Lena can **move first**, perhaps into teacher training.
With robots around **2034**, I can become the farm's robot person.

S3.quote: Five years sounds long, but courses fill up once everyone's scared.
fieldNote: Five years lets the household **sequence** changes: Lena first, then her.
She treats robots as a **job route** rather than a threat.

steps.text: Complete a two-year part-time farm robotics course
Get the trust to buy a robot weeder by 2029
Set up a regional co-op of land trusts to share machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I like this one, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can get it right: public training, community-owned machines, and farmers who know how to use them. I'd say small farms could thrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years makes this a good story for me. By 2039 I'd be 40 and could be running a whole farm with machines, maybe my own small one. Lena has years to change careers calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Hollin and bring in machines step by step: the weeder, then robot hen house cleaning. I'd buy a £500 community share in the land trust's new farm plan. And I'd keep learning the AI tools, because the people who know them will run the farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. A bit uneasy for people around me who don't like change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our volunteer coordinator, Frank, is 63 and won't touch a smartphone. Frank's brilliant with people, and I'd worry the farm forgets that's a job too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your own plans with Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably buy a small place in Thornby around 2030 instead of waiting. If the change is slow enough, it's safe to put down roots.

I'd argue **small farms** could thrive with community-owned machines.

Lena has **years** to change careers calmly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for me so much, for Lena and for us as a household. What would help is free retraining that starts the minute the news breaks, and a basic income so families don't fall through the cracks while they change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets to decide. A farm owned by the community can choose to keep people on even when robots are cheaper. A farm owned by a fund never will.

headlineQuote: A farm owned by the community can choose to keep people on even when robots are cheaper.
portrait: Priya is a 27-year-old **growing and livestock lead** at a community land trust farm.
She uses **AI daily** and sees robots as a route into new work.
Her biggest risk is her partner Lena's **claims office** job, which is very exposed.
She moves from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
She wants machines **owned by communities**, and plans to run them herself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Lena's job would go first and leave Priya the only earner.
whatWouldHelp: **Free retraining** that starts the moment the news breaks.
A **basic income** so households can change work without falling through.
